en: The Priyadarśikā, composed by Śrī Harṣadeva.

[Verse 1] Her vision clouded by smoke, her eyes refreshed once more by the rays of the moon, she gazes again upon her chosen lord with her face bowed in longing, yet overcome once more by shame before Brahmā.

May Gaurī bring you auspiciousness— she who, out of jealousy, had her hair standing on end from the touch of Hara as he held her hand, while she was looking at the reflection of the moon on his toenails in which the Gaṅgā appeared.
Moreover:
When Mount Kailāsa had risen up and the Gaṇas were moving about with surging curiosity,
while the Destroyer of Poison (Śiva) looked on in wrath as Kumāra entered his mother’s lap;

May Śiva protect us—he who, though enraged, was embraced by Umā as her body sank into the depths of the netherworld due to the weight of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa’s feet pressing down upon him; he who, being thus pleased, dispelled the thick cloud of fear. HPri_1.2 //
(At the end of the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* walks around the stage.

Today, at the spring festival, I was summoned with great honor by the assembly of kings who have come from various regions and provinces to serve at the lotus feet of His Majesty King Śrī Harṣadeva, and they said to me as follows: "By our Lord..."
We have heard through oral tradition that the illustrious King Harṣadeva composed a short play (*nāṭikā*) titled *Priyadarśikā*, adorned with the construction of an unprecedented plot;
however, we have not seen it performed.
"Therefore, out of great respect for that very king who gladdens the hearts of all people, and with the intention of showing us favor, you must perform this drama exactly as it is composed.
So then, having arranged the costumes, I shall accomplish what is desired."
Looking around:
"It is my conviction that the minds of the audience have been won over. Why?
Because Śrī Harṣa is a skillful poet, and this assembly is one that appreciates merit."
The life-story of King Vatsarāja is captivating to the world, and we are skilled in dramatic performance;

even a single one of these things here is a means for attaining desired results, so how much more so this entire collection of virtues, brought together through the abundance of my good fortune! (HPri 1.3)

(Looking toward the tiring-room) Ah! How is it that while I am about to begin the prologue, my brother— having understood our intention and assuming the role of the chamberlain to Dṛḍhavarman, the lord of Aṅga— is approaching from this very direction?
Therefore, I too shall prepare the stage for the next scene.
(Exit.
Thus ends the prologue.)
[Page 4] Act One.
(Then enters the chamberlain.)
Chamberlain—(Acting out grief and exhaustion;
sighing):
Alas! Oh, what misery! What misery!

The king’s suffering from the loss of his kinsmen, his exile from his kingdom, and his exhaustion on treacherous paths—these are the bitter and fruitless fruits that I have tasted for my long life. (HPri 1.4)
(With sorrow and wonder) Even though he was such a person— possessing the three powers unimpeded and equal to Raghu, Dilīpa, and Nala—
the King Dṛḍhavarman gave his own daughter to the King of Vatsa despite my entreaties; thus, filled with resentment, the King of Vatsa has been released from prison.

And as for the saying that "it does not turn back," it is truly inconceivable— even though it is logical— that such a calamity was brought about by that wretched Kalinga, who came suddenly having found an opening;
how could fate be so utterly cruel toward us?

Thinking, "By some means or other, having delivered her to the King of Vatsa, I shall free my master from his debt," I rescued that princess even from such a tumultuous assault as dreadful as the time of universal dissolution, and placed her in the house of King Vindhyaketu— an Āṭavika ruler who stands in friendship with His Majesty Dṛḍhavarman— where she remained not far away for the purpose of bathing.

Thus, while I had gone to the Agastyatīrtha, Vindhyaketu was struck down by certain people in an instant; the place was rendered devoid of humans as if by Rākṣasas, and when the site was burnt, it was not known in what state he remained.
I searched that entire location thoroughly.
Nor was it known whether she had been carried off by those very bandits or whether she had been burned;
what then shall I do, unfortunate as I am?
(Reflecting.)
Ah!
I have heard that the King of Vatsa, having escaped from captivity and carried off the daughter of Pradyota, has arrived at Kauśāmbī.
Shall I go there?
(Sighing and contemplating his own condition:
What indeed shall I say upon going there without the princess?
Alas!
And today Vindhyaketu told me: "Do not fear!
His Majesty the great king Dṛḍhavarman is alive; though shattered by severe blows, he remains bound."
Therefore, I shall now go to my master himself and make the remainder of my life fruitful by serving at his feet. (Walking about and looking upward) Oh, how extremely cruel is the autumn heat!
For even though I am thus tormented by manifold sufferings, this sharp [sun] is being endured by me.
Released from his dense bonds after the eclipse of the Maiden (Kanyā), the sun, having reached Libra (Tulā) and regained its own radiance, truly shines forth like King Vatsarāja.
(Thus he exits. (This concludes the interlude. (Then the King and the Vidūṣaka enter.)

The King: The unwavering devotion of my servants has been fully understood; the wisdom of my ministers has been observed; even my friends have been scrutinized; and the great affection of the citizens has been recognized.
My reckless addiction to battle has been brought to completion, and a jewel among women has been obtained as if through sincere dharma; what, indeed, have I not gained from this captivity?
Vidūṣaka: (With anger) O friend!

Why do you praise that very son of a slave, ruined by imprisonment? Have you now forgotten how the Queen herself was like a young bride, her feet stumbling and tripping against the bonds of the rattling iron chains?
With a heart tormented by the harshness of emptiness and suffering, with eyes wide open in the grip of rage, and with a path across the earth marked by heavy, forceful stampings,
you have experienced the misery of sleeplessness even during the nights.
[O friend!]
How can you praise that very son of a slave, that wretch of a prisoner?
You have now forgotten how he was like a newly captured lordly elephant, his feet stumbling against the bonds of the clanging iron chains.

"With the heat of your heart signaled by the lotus-like opening of your empty mouth, your gaze raised in the power of rage, and the path of the earth torn asunder by the heavy slapping of your hands—you have experienced no pleasure of sleep even during the nights.
The King said: "Vasantaka, you are indeed a wicked man! Behold!"
We have seen the prison, dense with darkness, yet not the radiance of her moon-like face;
we have heard the harsh sound of your fetters, yet not her sweet words;
the cruel guards of the prison are now in our minds, yet not her affectionate glances.
You perceive the faults of bondage, but not the virtues of Pradyota’s daughter.
Vidūṣaka: (Proudly) Oh!
If imprisonment were indeed a source of happiness, then why do you harbor resentment toward King Kaliṅga because Dṛḍhavarman has been imprisoned?
[O sir! If bondage is indeed the bond of happiness, then why do you, Dṛḍhavarman, being bound, harbor resentment toward the King of Kaliṅga? The King—(smiling):
"Fie on you, fool!
Not every King Vatsarāja, having obtained Vāsavadattā in this manner, would emerge from captivity.
So, let this matter rest for now."
Many days have passed since Vijayasena was dispatched against Vindhyaketu, yet even now no one has returned from his presence.
Therefore, let the minister Rumaṇvat be summoned;
I wish to speak with him for a while.
(Entering) Chamberlain:
Victory, victory to Your Majesty!
Here indeed are the minister Vijayasena and Rumaṇvan, arrived at the entrance hall.
"Victory, victory to the King! Indeed, this minister Vijayasena and Rumaṇvat have arrived at the entrance. The King: "Admit them quickly."
Portress: As Your Majesty commands. (Exit.)
(Then enter Rumaṇvān and Vijayasena.
Rumaṇvān—(Reflecting:
They have departed even for a moment, as if they had committed an offense, though no offense was committed.
Servants generally enter the royal palace apprehensive.
(Approaching) Victory to the King!
The King— (Pointing to a seat) Rumaṇvat!
"Please, sit here. Rumaṇvān— (sitting down with a smile)—
"This indeed is Vijayasena, who has conquered Vindhyaketu."
He bows down.
(Vijayasena does likewise.
The King—(embracing him respectfully)—:
"Are you well?
Vijayasena replied, "Today, by the grace of my lord.
The King said, "Vijayasena, please be seated."
[Vijayasena sits down.
King: Vijayasena, tell me the news concerning Vindhyaketu.
Vijayasena: My Lord, what more shall I say? Such is the state when the Master is enraged.
The King: Nevertheless, I wish to hear it in detail.
Vijayasena said: "Your Majesty, please listen.

Following the command of Your Majesty's feet, we have traversed even a great distance in three days with our elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers reduced to such wretchedness as was ordered; then, at the hour of dawn, we descended unexpectedly upon Vindhyaketu."
The King: And then? What happened next?

Vijayasena: Then, upon hearing the tumultuous clamor of our army, that Vindhyaketu—like a lion awakened from his lair in the Vindhya caves—emerged, disregarding his troops and vehicles, accompanied only by whatever few companions were at hand.
Suddenly proclaiming his own name, he has begun to attack us.
The King— (looking at Rumaṇvat, with a smile)—
Vindhyaketu has acted with distinction.
And so it went.

Vijayasena said: "Then, with our resentment and zeal redoubled by the thought, 'This is he!'—and through a great struggle in which all our allies were exhausted—he alone, having crushed the force of the enemy's superior strength and fury, delivered a most terrible blow."
The King: Well done, Vindhyaketu!
Well done, well done!
Vijayasena: What more can be said, Your Majesty?
I shall report briefly:

having first crushed the infantry right where they stood with a mere press of his chest and driven them far away, he scattered the cavalry in all directions with showers of arrows like a terrified herd of deer.

Having cast aside his entire collection of weapons in every respect, he quickly drew his sword and proceeded to perform, as if in play, the severing of an elephant’s trunk and a grove of plantain trees.
Thus, alone and making the three forces disordered, his shoulder-blades were streaked by the rays of his sword,
while his thighs and chest were shattered by hundreds of blows from weapons.
Exhausted after a long time, Vindhyaketu was struck down in battle.
The King: Rumaṇvat!
Truly, as we follow the path befitting a virtuous man, we are indeed ashamed by the death of Vindhyaketu.
Rumaṇvat: Your Majesty, for those such as yourself who are solely partial toward virtue, even the virtues of an enemy produce joy.
The King: Vijayasena, is there also an offspring of Vindhyaketu, wherein I may show the fruit of my satisfaction?
Vijayasena: Your Majesty, I shall inform you of this as well.
When Vindhyaketu has been slain along with his kinsmen and retinue, and when his wives, who followed him, have taken refuge on the peaks of the Vindhya mountains—

Now that the countryside has been laid waste, a maiden of noble birth—fitting for the lineage of Vindhyaketu—stands at our gate, having been brought by us from his palace; she utters piteous lamentations, "Alas, father! Alas, mother! in that desolate place.
Your Majesty is the sole authority regarding her.
The King: Yaśodharā, go;
you yourself deliver her to Vāsavadattā.
And the goddess should be addressed thus:
"She must always be regarded by you with the thought that she is your sister;
she should be instructed in everything appropriate for an exceptional maiden, such as singing, dancing, instrumental music, and so forth."
"When she becomes marriageable, then remind me. The female doorkeeper replied, "As Your Majesty commands.
[Whatever Your Majesty orders.]
(Thus she exits.
(Behind the scenes, a bard:
[To those] who provide the requisites for the auspicious bath, such as the immersion in playful pastimes...

Now, the bathing ground for you— adorned by the breasts of all the women of the inner apartments who possess every grace, their shadows unobstructed as their silken garments slip from them due to exertion—
is like a place beautified by other golden jars set upon it.
The King—(looking upward):
Ah! How is it that the blessed Lord of a thousand rays has already taken his seat in the midst of the sky?
For now:
The water of the pond shines as if boiling from the heat of the sun’s rays, with the leaping of its fish;
meanwhile, the peacock spreads its mass of plumage, which resembles a parasol, though it is loosened by the play of his dancing.
The young fawn, greedy for the water in the basin, approaches the circle of shadows cast by the trees;
the bee, instantly abandoning the elephant's cheek, enters the fold of its ear.
Rumaṇvat: Rise, rise!
Having entered the inner apartments and performed the appropriate rites, let us honor Vijayasena and dispatch him for the destruction of the Kaliṅgas.
(Thus they all exit.)
(Thus ends the first act.
Vidūṣaka: I have been told by Indīvarikā that Queen Vāsavadattā, who is observing a fast for the vow of the eleventh day, summons me to offer her congratulations.
Therefore, having bathed in the pond of the fountain-house garden, I shall go to the Queen's side and perform the "cock-fight" (a ritual).
Otherwise, how could Brahmins like us receive alms in a royal household?
(Looking toward the tiring-room)
Where is my dear friend? Today he has gone to the fountain garden specifically to dispel the longing caused by his separation from the Queen.
Therefore, I shall go with my friend and perform as instructed.
[Indeed, I was told by Indivarikā that Queen Vāsavadattā, who is observing a vow of fasting, has requested me to announce her name for the sake of reciting benedictions.]
Therefore, having bathed in the fountain of the shower-house garden and gone to the Queen's side, I shall engage in a cockfight;

otherwise, how could we Brahmins, who are her equals, accept gifts at the royal court? (Looking toward the dressing room) Why has my dear friend departed today for the very shower-house garden, for the purpose of dispelling the longing born of separation from the Queen?
Therefore, I shall go together with my friend and carry out what has been said.
(Then the King enters, full of longing.)
The King: [Behold] her, emaciated, wearing only auspicious ornaments, speaking with faint effort, her face— pale in complexion— having surpassed the splendor of the morning moon.

My heart yearns to see her, who is herself longing [for me], through the practice of vows and fasting— just as one longs for a beloved woman today who has fallen into the state produced by their first passion.
Vidūṣaka— (Approaching) Prosperity to you! May your honor prosper!
[May it be well with you! May the Blessed One prosper!
The King—(looking around)—Vasantaka!
"Why do you appear as if so delighted?
Vidūṣaka: "The Queen is indeed honoring a Brahmin."
The King: If that is so, then what of it?
Vidūṣaka: (Proudly) Oh!
Such indeed is this Brāhmaṇa, who, at the very beginning, [was introduced] into the royal court crowded with thousands of Brāhmaṇas learned in the four Vedas, five Vedas, and six Vedas.
I myself shall obtain a message of well-being from the presence of the Queen.
[O! Such indeed is this Brahmin.]
"And I alone am the first to receive the benediction from the presence of the Goddess in a lineage of Ṛg-veda priests crowded with thousands of Brāhmaṇas learned in four, five, or six Vedas.
The King— (smiling)—
"The status of a Brāhmaṇa has been made known by the very number of the Vedas."
Therefore come, Great Brahmin;
let us go to the fountain-house garden.
Vidūṣaka: As Your Majesty commands.
"As Your Majesty commands.
The King said: "Go on ahead.
Vidūṣaka: Friend, come, let us go.
(Walking about and looking around) Friend, look, look!

The splendor of this fountain-house garden, where the surfaces of the stone slabs are soft with various flowers falling incessantly, where the clusters of *bākulamālātī* trees are broken by the weight of bees clinging to their fragrance, where the winds are unrestrained in seizing the scent of lotuses,
where the *bandhūka* flowers are bound together, and where the sunlight is shielded by dense *tamāla* trees.
[My friend, come, let us go. (Walking about and looking around) My friend, look, look!

Of this [place], whose stone surfaces are soft with various flowers falling incessantly; where the clusters of *bakula* and *mālatī* creepers are broken by the weight of bees clinging to their fragrance;
where the opening of the *bandhūka* blossoms is awakened by the wind powerful in seizing the scent of lotuses; and where the light of the sun is obscured by the dense shade of *tamāla* trees.
[The splendor of the fountain-house garden.
The King: Friend, you have spoken well. For here, the ground appears as if covered by the stalks of *śephālikā* flowers with their tiny new shoots.

The fragrance of the *saptacchada* trees instantly causes a stupor through its intoxication with the scent of elephant ichor; and here, bees— drunk from drinking wine (*vāruṇī*), their bodies anointed yellow by the thick mass of pollen falling from blossoming lotuses— hum something indistinctly.
Vidūṣaka: Oh, friend!
Look, look at this too!

This saptaparṇa tree, from which clusters of flowers are falling incessantly, still appears as if it were dripping with drops of water at the end of the rainy season through the interstices of its leaves.
"O friend, look, look at this as well!
This *saptaparṇa* tree, with its mass of flowers falling incessantly, still appears like a drop of water from the end of the rainy season trickling down the edge of a leaf.
The King: "Friend, you have imagined it perfectly."
It is indeed very much like the season of the clouds; for instance:
the grassy meadows, possessing softness and captivating with the beauty of *śirīṣa* flowers, have suddenly formed paved courtyards as if washed with powdered emeralds.
Now, this earth appears as if still covered by hundreds of *indragopa* insects, with heaps of *bandhūka* flowers fallen from their stalks.
(Then enters a maidservant.
Maidservant: I have been commanded by Queen Vāsavadattā:
"O girl Indīvarikā, today I must present an offering to the great seer Agastya."
Therefore, go;
take a garland of *sehālikā* flowers quickly and return.

This Āraṇṇikā too must come after having plucked the lotuses from the stream of the fountain-garden as soon as they have blossomed, before they are closed by the sun who desires them no longer. Go quickly!
Thus it is;
this ascetic woman does not know that it is long.
Therefore, having taken it, I shall go.
(Looking toward the tiring-room) This way, this way, Āraṇṇikā! Come here.
I have been commanded by Queen Vāsavadattā.
"O maiden Indīvarikā, today I must offer the arghya water to the great seer Agastya.
Therefore, go;
take a garland of śephālikā flowers quickly and return."
"This Āraṇyikā too— while the lotuses in the pond of the garden-house are still in bloom and have not yet been closed by the sun longing for its setting— let her come quickly and without thought.
This poor woman does not know about that pond.
"Taking that, I shall go there. [Looking toward the tiring-room] (Then enters Āraṇyikā).
Āraṇyikā—(With tears and agitation, to herself)
Indeed, for one born into such a lineage and remaining there after making herself known to others, it is not at all difficult for fate to now command her to serve another.
Or rather, this is my own fault, since even though I knew [the truth], I did not kill myself. So, what shall I do now?
Or rather, what I have thought now is difficult; it would have been better not to have revealed my own noble lineage at all, thereby making myself appear insignificant. So, what is to be done?
I shall do as it has been said. (With agitation and tears, to herself:
"That I, born into such a lineage, having remained by commanding other people, must now carry out the command of another—truly, there is nothing difficult for Fate."
Or rather, this is my own fault, that even though I knew it, I did not destroy myself.
So, what shall I do now?
Or perhaps I have now conceived a difficult task.
This is indeed better;
for by revealing my own highly noble lineage, I have not diminished myself.
What other recourse is there?
"I shall carry out exactly as you have said.
Maid: "Come this way, Āraṇyikā! "Come this way, Āraṇyikā!"
Āraṇyikā: Here I come.
(Acting out exhaustion) Friend, why is the road still so long even now?
[Here I come.
(Acting out exhaustion) "Friend, why is the oblong pond still so far away even now?"
Maid: She is hidden within a cluster of *śephālikā* shrubs;
come, let us descend. (They both act out descending.)
[This is hidden by a thicket of *śephālikā* shrubs; come, let us descend. (They both act out descending.)
The King: Friend, why do you seem to be thinking of something else?
Am I not saying that this is indeed very much like the rainy season?
(He recites again, beginning with "Bearing softness," etc.)
Vidūṣaka: (Angrily) Oh!
You are indeed diverting yourself with this other thing, completely filled with longing;
but for me, a Brahmin, the time for the auspicious benediction is passing away.
Therefore, while I hasten to bathe in the pond and go to the Queen's presence—
[with anger]— oh, you there, while you are looking at this and that, you amuse yourself with overflowing longing;
but for me, a Brahmin, the time for the recitation of benedictions is passing away!
"Therefore, while I am still here, I shall quickly bathe in the long pond and go to the presence of the Queen.
The King: "But you fool, we have already reached the far shore of the long pond!"
Thus, even while experiencing such a multitude of supreme pleasures of the senses, you do not perceive them; look!

This swan’s cry, sounding like the tinkling of a beloved’s anklets, brings joy to the ear; and the palace turret, partially visible through the gaps in the trees on the bank, bestows delight upon the sight.
The fragrance of lotuses, potent with its perfume, brings pleasure to the sense of smell;
these breezes, cooled by contact with water, bestow delight upon the limbs.
Come then, let us approach the bank of the long pond.
(Walking about and looking around) Friend, look, look!
Like the clear gaze of the garden goddess, charming with the beauty of a blooming lotus,
this long eye-lash delights me by its very sight.
Vidūṣaka: (With curiosity) Oh friend, look, look!

Who is this woman, whose braid of hair is fragrant with the scent of flowers and swarms with bees, whose hand-palms are like coral and young shoots, and whose arms are like bright, slender, and tender creepers—she is truly like a garden goddess appearing before our very eyes!
It is seen. [With curiosity] O friend, look, look!

"Who is this woman seen here, appearing like the garden goddess herself in visible form— she who has a braid fragrant with the scent of flowers and bees, whose sprout-like hands are as red as coral creepers, and whose arms are like radiant, tender, and delicate vines?
The King— (looking with curiosity)—
Friend, she who has given rise to many conjectures through the splendor of her unsurpassed natural beauty—truly, even I do not understand her; look!
"Has some Naga maiden risen from the underworld, intent on beholding the world?
That was surely seen by me in vain; for how could such a one exist there? Could she be the Moonlight (Kaumudī) incarnate here? But her being seen during the day is not possible."
Who is this woman who is being gazed upon by him with a lotus held in the palm of his hand, as if she were Śrī herself?
Vidūṣaka: (Observing) This is indeed Indīvarikā, the attendant of the Queen.
Therefore, let us hide behind this bush and watch.
[Having observed: "This is indeed Indīvarikā, the attendant of the Queen.
Therefore, let us hide behind this thicket and watch.
(Both do so.)
Maid: (Acting out the gathering of lotus leaves) Forest-dweller, please take these lotuses for yourself.
I too, having gathered these *śephālikā* flowers upon this lotus leaf, shall go to the Queen's presence.
(Acting out the gathering of the lotus leaves:
Āraṇyikā, you gather the lotuses.
"I too shall gather śephālikā flowers upon this lotus leaf and go into the presence of the Queen.
The King: "Friend, it is as if we are engaged in conversation. Therefore, let us listen attentively."
"Perhaps it will become clear from this very point.
(The maidservant mimes departing.
Āraṇyikā: "Friend Indīvarikā, I cannot remain here for even a moment without you."
"O Indīvarikā!
I cannot remain here even for a moment without you.
Maid: (Laughing)
"Since I have heard such counsel from the Queen today as this, you must remain separated from me for a long time indeed.
(Laughing) "Since I have heard such counsel from the Queen today as this, you must remain separated from me for a long time indeed.
Āraṇyikā— (with dejection) What has the Queen deliberated?

Maid: Indeed. At that time, I was told by the Great King: "When this daughter of Vindhya-ketu becomes fit for marriage, you must remind me. Therefore, I shall now remind him, so that he will become overwhelmed with thoughts regarding her marriage.
Therefore, O Great King, I was told by you: "When this daughter of Vindhyaketu becomes marriageable, then I am to be reminded.
Thus, I now remind the Great King, so that he will become preoccupied with thoughts regarding her suitor.
The King—(with joy):
This is that daughter of Vindhyaketu.
(With remorse) We have been deceived for a long time;
friend, this maiden is indeed one whose innocence is evident.
"Now let us look with confidence. Āraṇyikā— (angrily covering her ears) Then go away!
I have no need for you, who prattle on so incoherently;
therefore, go away! [Therefore, go;
I have no use for you, who prattle on so incoherently.]
(The maidservant steps aside and mimes gathering flowers.
King: Oh, her noble birth is all the more clearly revealed by her composure!
Friend, truly fortunate is he who shall become the recipient of the pleasure of touching these limbs.
(Āraṇyikā mimes the act of gathering lotuses.
Vidūṣaka: Oh, friend! Look, look!
A marvel, a marvel!
Gathering lotuses, she brings a laughing splendor to the lotus grove by means of the radiance spreading from her sprout-like hands trembling in the water.
[O friend, look, look!
A marvel, a marvel!]
Gathering lotuses, she puts to shame the splendor of the lotus grove with the radiance spreading from her hand-stalks shimmering in the water.
The King: Friend, this is indeed true; look!
Bestowing upon the eyes an indescribable state of visibility— like a continuous rain of nectar-drops, yet with the veil of her breasts slipping away—
the woman has become a fit object for the touch of his hands, just as the body of the moon becomes the locus for the rays of that same moon.
It is truly a marvel that these lotuses suddenly close their buds.
Āraṇyikā—(Acting out the harassment by bees) Alas, alas!
These other wicked bees, abandoning the lotus pond, are now falling upon the groves of blue water-lilies; harassing me with their swarms, they cause me distress.
(Covering her face with her upper garment, in fear) Friend Indīvarikā, save me! Save me! These wicked bees are indeed going to overwhelm me.
(Acting out the harassment by bees) Alas, woe! Woe!

Indeed, these others, abandoning the lotus pond and rushing toward the groves of blue water-lilies, harass me even more intensely as they torment me. (Covering her face with her upper garment, in fear)
"O Indīvarikā, save me! Save me!
These wicked bees will surely overwhelm me!
Vidūṣaka: "O friend, your desires have been fulfilled!"
"As long as the daughter of the slave-girl does not arrive, you too must approach in silence.
Knowing that Indīvarikā is coming by the path along the water indicated by the sound of the splashing, she will surely hang upon you.
[Friend, your desires are fulfilled.]
"As long as the son of the slave-girl Garbhadāsī has not yet arrived, you too must approach him silently.
Knowing that Indīvarikā is coming by the sound of her footsteps revealed by the splashing of water, she will surely lean upon you.
The King said: "Excellent, friend, excellent!"
"It has been taught in accordance with the time.
(Thus, he approaches the hermitage.)
Āraṇyikā—(Acting as if she has heard the sound of footsteps) Indīvarikā!
Come quickly, come quickly!
I am being harassed by wicked bees! (She clings to the King.)
"Indīvarikā, come quickly, come quickly!
I have been harassed by wicked bees!
(The King takes her by the neck.)
(Removing her forest-dweller’s upper garment from her face and not seeing the king, she acts out the appearance of bees.
